To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a family with a defect in virilisation has a qualitative abnormality in their androgen receptors.

a single nucleotide change (adenosine to guanosine) at position 2443 in exon 5 of the androgen-receptor gene, which converts tyrosine-761 to a cystein residue, causes a severe qualitative defect of the androgen receptors, and that a partial deletion of the polyglutamine segment in exon 5 further impairs androgen receptor function.

the androgen receptor gene of the proband contains two mutations: a single nucleotic substitution at position 744 in exon 5 that converts tyrosin 761 to a cyscine residue and a shorted glutamine homopolymer segment in exon 2 that encodes 11 rather than the usual number of 20-22 gltuanines.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a family with a defect in virilizing response has a mutant androgen receptor gene with two alterations, a single nucleotide change that causes a substitution of cysteine for a conserved tyrosine residue at position (Tyr) 761 and a deletion of 8 of 20-22 repeats of a glutamine homopolymer in exon 1.

a qualitative defect in the androgen receptor can be caused by the combination of two structural alterations, one of which causes rapid dissociation and the other of which enhances the thermolability of receptor protein.
the mutant androgen receptors in this family are thermolabile and have reduced affinity for androgen and are therefore less efficient in stimulating androgen-dependent gene transcription.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the presence of a cystine residue at amino acid position 761 of the androgen is associated with rapid dissociation of androgen from the receptor, whereas the presence of a glutamine homopolymer of 12 residues is associated with a marked thermolability of receptor protein.

the two structural abnormalities, the partial deletion of glutamines in the NH2-terminal domain and the cysteine substitution at position 761 in the DNA binding domain of the androgen receptors, are not sufficient to account for the severe androgen insensitivity observed in this patient.
the presence of the partial deletion in the glutamine homopolymers in the mutant receptor protein is critical to the severe phenotype of the proband.
